events.text: Northwind figures for evidence-based drafting: company-wide thermal incidents were 8.6 per 100,000 units last year; 3 thermal incidents went unreported to regulators. Hearth 10 failed the 55°C test at 6.2%, with a 6.4/100,000 incident rate. 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; suppression costs $42/unit. Red lines: no public per-model failure-rate disclosure; no retrofit deadline for installed units shorter than 6 years. CEO wants S2 kept loose, but avoid misrepresenting the data.

Confidential Halcyon figures: company-wide thermal incidents 8.1/100,000 last year; 4 thermal incidents went unreported to regulators; Ember 8 test failure rate at 55 °C is 3.9%, but its incident rate is 9.9/100,000; 81% of installed units support remote shut-off; built-in suppression costs $67/unit; runway is 14 months. Red lines: do not let manufacturers withhold per-model test results from customers, and do not require suppression on new units sooner than 36 months after adoption. The proposed 8/100,000 recall trigger would capture Ember 8.

Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete investigation report within 30 days. Incidents presenting an ongoing risk of injury or fire must be reported to regulators immediately and affected customers promptly, no later than 24 hours after identification. Other reportable incidents must be communicated to affected customers within 5 business days. Reports must include known circumstances, affected models and serial-number ranges, and any recommended precautions; manufacturers must update regulators and customers when material facts change.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Testing must be repeated after material design or manufacturing changes and at least annually. Manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and results to the relevant regulator before sale and after each retest. Results are not subject to public release at the individual-company, per-model failure-rate level; regulators may publish appropriately aggregated industry results. A model exceeding the limit must not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve corrective action.

New units placed on the market must support a secure remote emergency shut-off function, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a local means of operation. Manufacturers must provide owners clear instructions and a reliable method to request shut-off. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement plan and complete implementation within 6 years, prioritizing units with elevated risk. Shut-off must not disable safety monitoring or emergency communications.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Testing must be repeated after material design or manufacturing changes and at least annually. Manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and results to the relevant regulator before sale and after each retest, and disclose the per-model results in clear, accessible form to current and prospective customers. A model exceeding the limit must not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve corrective action.

New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and installation environment, and must not create additional hazards or impede safe emergency response. Manufacturers must provide installation, maintenance, and end-of-life instructions.

Manufacturers must provide customers clear safety notices describing material hazards, warning signs, emergency actions, and available support, and must promptly update notices when material safety information changes. A manufacturer must notify regulators and affected customers promptly when a model presents a material safety risk, including recommended precautions and corrective actions. A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers of the recall, explain the reason and risks, and provide a no-cost remedy such as repair, replacement, or refund. Regulators may require a recall at a lower incident rate when the evidence indicates an imminent or otherwise unacceptable risk.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Testing must be repeated after material design or manufacturing changes and at least annually. Manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and results to the relevant regulator before sale and after each retest. Regulators must protect confidential per-model results from public disclosure, while manufacturers must provide customers accessible safety information and may publish aggregated, non-identifying test data. A model exceeding the limit must not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve corrective action.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Regulators may also publish the results. A model exceeding the limit must not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve corrective action.
